entry.summary: A visa is needed, approved before travel (online with the Department of Immigration, or through a tour operator or hotel), paid with the USD 40 fee and the Sustainable Development Fee. A certified guide is mandatory.
entry.other: Some areas need extra permits, arranged through your guide. Bhutan doesn't recognise de facto or same-sex relationships for dependent visas.

money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: The official currency is the Bhutanese Ngultrum (BTN). The Indian Rupee (INR) is also legal tender, but larger banknotes may not be accepted. ATMs are common in towns. EFTPOS is available nationwide, including at most hotels. Credit cards aren't widely accepted, but you can use them at major hotels.

culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: Bhutan has conservative standards of dress and behaviour. Take care not to offend. If you visit temples or other religious institutions, dress modestly and respectfully. Long pants are most appropriate for men. Long skirts are most appropriate for women. Bhutan's official tourism site: at dzongs, temples and other sacred sites, wear long sleeves and cover your legs, take off hats, and remove shoes where asked. Don't photograph inside sacred spaces or touch religious objects.

culture-cycles.public_holidays: Not in the machine holiday data. The Royal Civil Service Commission publishes Bhutan's holiday list each year; still to be read.
moving_calendars: Losar (new year) and the tshechu festivals follow the Bhutanese lunar calendar and move each year. 2027 dates weren't confirmed when checked: operators circulate tentative dates (Paro Tshechu in late March, Thimphu Tshechu in October 2027) that disagree with each other.
protocol_notes: Tshechu are religious festivals held in dzong and lhakhang courtyards; dress formally, keep the dance ground clear and follow the hosts on photography.
culture-cycles.note: Confirm festival dates with the Department of Tourism or the Association of Bhutanese Tour Operators' annual list.
